title: Can Free Will Justify It?
hook: If the alternative is endless torment, is choosing God really a free choice?
tldr: "People choose hell" fails: a choice made under threat of infinite torment is coercion, not freedom. A loving parent fences off the highway, the Torah never punished beyond death, and our minds are too shaped by wounds and influences to deserve infinite judgment. Love cannot be forced; God rescues rather than abandons.
big_idea: A choice under threat of endless torment is coercion, not free will.

points.title: A gun to the soul
points.text: A choice made under existential fear is forced, like signing with a knife at your throat, or an abuser saying "If you don't love me, I'll burn you, but it's your choice."

points.title: Loving parents fence the highway
points.text: A decent parent does not let toddlers play by a highway, warn once, and say "that's on you." They build a fence or remove the danger. Doing otherwise is negligence or cruelty.

points.title: The Torah never punished without end
points.text: Its harshest penalty was swift death, rarely carried out, never torture or afterlife suffering. Moses, David and Paul all committed grave sins and found redemption.

points.title: Our minds are not fully free
points.text: We are shaped by wounds, fears, culture, upbringing and even demonic voices. "Ideas have people." Infinite punishment would require perfect freedom and clarity that only God has.

points.title: Love cannot be forced
points.text: Perfect love casts out fear. Any gospel saying "forgiven, but only if..." is not the gospel. Christ took away the sin of the world: no ifs, no buts.

points.title: God will gather every soul
points.text: God forces no one, yet no heart will withstand perfect love forever. Through Christ, God will find, heal and gather all, battered but beloved.

sections.summary: Eternal Conscious Torment has long been defended by free will: God does not send people to hell; they choose it. But a choice under threat of unending torment is not free; it is the worst coercion, like a gun to your head ordering you to your knees, or an abuser telling a captive, "If you don't love me, I'll burn you, but it's your choice."

sections.h: A father warning a child on the highway?
sections.summary: Some say we are toddlers on a busy highway whom the Father warns, leaving the choice to us. But what parent lets toddlers play by a highway? A loving one builds a fence, locks doors, holds hands, or removes the danger. Placing spiritually helpless children near an infinite consequence is negligence or cruelty. Millions die never hearing of Jesus meaningfully: who put them there? You would not torture your child for failing a theology test.

sections.h: The false choice: love or infinite suffering
sections.summary: A contract signed with a knife at one's throat is a choice to avoid suffering, not love. Hellfire theology puts a gun to the soul and calls it free will. If rejecting God means endless torment, there is only forced submission. A loving God would not watch us destroy ourselves forever; real love rescues. "Love me, or I'll make sure you fall into a pit of fire" is extortion; an infinite penalty makes the choice illegitimate.

sections.h: Even in the Torah, punishment had an end
sections.summary: The Law's harshest penalty was death, swift, not torture, ending with this life: a "game over" here, not everlasting torment. If torment were just, why not in the Torah? Its system was restrained, rarely executing, proportional and merciful, unlike prolonged pagan punishments, with no threat of afterlife suffering. Moses murdered, David arranged a murder, Paul persecuted Christians; all were redeemed. Free will is a reason to transform us, not condemn us.

sections.h: Fear-based love is not love at all
sections.summary: "Perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18), yet eternal conscious torment depends and thrives on fear; hellfire theology rests on existential terror. If God desires a loving relationship, why make fear the main motivator? Affection given under threat of hellfire is survival at best. Free will without true alternatives is meaningless.

sections.h: How free is our mind, anyway?
sections.summary: Perfectly just judgment needs perfectly free, unbiased minds, which we lack. We are shaped by every experience, wound, fear and voice, even demonic ones. In an age of social media and podcasts, how many thoughts are our own? Jordan Peterson cites Carl Jung: "People don't have ideas, ideas have people," and says 95% of what we think and say does not originate from our true selves.

sections.h: No fair verdict of infinite punishment
sections.summary: If judgment is shaped by wounds we did not choose, fears, malevolent spiritual forces, culture, upbringing, genetics, personality and pressures, infinite torment would be monstrously unjust. Everlasting hellfire requires perfect clarity, freedom and objectivity, which only God has. A God of perfect justice could not and would not burn confused, wounded, influence-shaped humans forever for limited decisions.

God's love should exceed human love. A loving God would offer endless chances for reconciliation, even in the age to come (Matthew 18:21-22); heal, not inflict pain (Luke 5:31-32); aim at restoration (2 Corinthians 5:18-19); desire genuine love, not compliance (Romans 8:38-39); and never build a system on terror (Lamentations 3:31-32). Love must be freely given, as C.S. Lewis said. "You are forgiven if..." is a lie.

sections.h: The gospel: no ifs, no buts
sections.summary: Through Christ God has "taken away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). No ifs, no buts, just a period. He is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2:2). God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting people's sins against them (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).

sections.h: Conclusion: all gathered into His embrace
sections.summary: Christianity must abandon the abusive Augustinian-Calvinist framework for the God of Israel shown by Jesus. God forces no one, but everyone will freely conclude; no knee will remain unbowed. However prodigal, Christ will find us, bandage our wounds and guide us back, even through regret, "gnashing of teeth" and resistance. No heart withstands perfect love forever. If your theology makes God less loving than the parent you aspire to be, rethink it.

mythfact.myth: God doesn't send anyone to hell; people freely choose it.
mythfact.fact: A choice made under threat of unending torment is coerced, like signing a contract with a knife at your throat.

mythfact.myth: God is like a father warning toddlers not to run into traffic.
mythfact.fact: A loving parent would never let toddlers play by a highway; they would fence it off or remove the danger.

mythfact.myth: Eternal torment reflects the justice of God's Law.
mythfact.fact: The Torah's harshest penalty was swift death, rarely used, with no threat of endless afterlife suffering.

mythfact.myth: Our choices are free enough to deserve infinite judgment.
mythfact.fact: Our minds are shaped by wounds, culture and outside voices; infinite punishment would need perfect freedom that only God has.

terms.meaning: The Augustinian-Calvinist view that the damned suffer consciously and unendingly in hell.
A choice forced by threat; telling someone they will burn unless they believe is its very definition.
Carl Jung's observation, cited by Jordan Peterson, that most of our thoughts come from outside influences.

quotes.text: If free will is exercised under the threat of unending torment, then it is not free at all.
Human free will—our stupidity and stubbornness—is not an excuse to condemn us to eternal torment, but rather a reason to transform us.
If your theology portrays God as less loving or caring than the parent you aspire to be, it’s time to rethink that theology.

verses.role: Perfect love casts out fear, yet eternal torment thrives on fear.
Endless opportunities for reconciliation, even in the age to come.
God brings healing, not endless pain.
God reconciles the world, not counting sins against them.
God desires genuine love, not forced compliance.
God would never create a system of terror and perpetual suffering.
Christ took away the sin of the world: no ifs, no buts.
Atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world.

quiz.q: What does the knife-at-the-throat illustration show?
options: A choice made to avoid suffering is not a free choice of love
quiz.why: Hellfire theology places a gun to the soul and calls it free will; a choice under infinite threat is coercion.

quiz.q: What was the harshest punishment in the Torah?
options: The death penalty, swift and rarely carried out
quiz.why: The Law never prescribed perpetual torture or afterlife suffering; punishment ended with this life.

quiz.q: What share of our thoughts does Peterson say do not originate from our true selves?
quiz.why: Peterson says 95% of what we think and say comes from outside, so our wills are not free enough for infinite judgment.

reflect: Would you call a choice free if one option carried a penalty of endless agony?
